items.followUp: Define a closed system and give one example.

rubric.why: The definition must state that no external force acts on the system.
rubric.description: States the defining condition of an isolated system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the system experiences no external force.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example, such as two colliding bodies treated as an isolated system.

modelAnswer: An isolated system is a system on which no external force acts.
Example: Two colliding bodies on a smooth surface may be considered an isolated system.

items.followUp: What force keeps a planet in its orbit around the Sun? Write the expression for this force.

rubric.why: Earth's gravitational attraction supplies the centripetal force needed to keep the satellite in orbit.
rubric.description: Identifies the force providing centripetal force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Earth's gravitational force provides it.

rubric.why: The centripetal force has magnitude mv²/r and is equal to the gravitational force for the satellite's orbit.
rubric.description: Gives the value or expression for the force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct expression, such as F = mv²/r (equal to GMm/r²).

modelAnswer: Earth's gravitational force provides the centripetal force for an artificial satellite.
Its value is F = mv²/r, which is equal to the gravitational force GMm/r².

items.followUp: Sketch or describe the speed-time graph for a body moving at constant speed.

rubric.why: A variable speed is represented by a speed-time graph that is not a horizontal straight line; for changing speed it is generally curved.
rubric.description: States the shape of the graph.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a curved or non-straight graph.

accept: unequal distances in equal time intervals
rubric.why: The explanation should connect the graph's shape with the changing speed.
rubric.description: Briefly explains why the graph has that shape.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that speed changes with time.

modelAnswer: The speed-time graph of a body moving with variable speed is generally a curved line.
Its speed changes with time, so the graph is not a horizontal straight line.

items.followUp: Define oscillatory motion and give one example.

rubric.why: Vibratory motion involves repeated motion in opposite directions.
rubric.description: States the to-and-fro nature of vibratory motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing repeated to-and-fro or back-and-forth motion.

rubric.why: The motion is about a mean position, and a suitable example completes the answer.
rubric.description: Mentions the mean position or gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning motion about a mean position or giving a suitable example.

modelAnswer: Vibratory motion is the repeated to-and-fro motion of a body about its mean position.
Example: The prongs of a tuning fork vibrate.

items.followUp: What are the main components of plasma? Give one example of where it is found.

rubric.why: Plasma is an ionized state of matter containing charged particles.
rubric.description: Defines plasma in terms of its ionized nature or particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an ionized gas or stating that it contains ions and free electrons.

rubric.why: A suitable example shows where plasma occurs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two valid examples.

modelAnswer: Plasma is an ionized gas consisting of positive ions and free electrons.

rubric.why: The principle applies to a body floating in a fluid.
rubric.description: Identifies the situation to which the principle applies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the principle concerns a floating body.

rubric.why: A floating body displaces fluid whose weight equals the body's weight.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the weight of the displaced fluid equals the weight of the floating body.

modelAnswer: A floating body displaces a fluid whose weight is equal to its own weight.
This statement is called the principle of flotation.

items.followUp: Describe one experiment that demonstrates atmospheric pressure.

rubric.why: The answer must state that air has weight or exerts pressure.
rubric.description: States that the atmosphere exerts pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying atmospheric pressure or the weight of air as the cause.

rubric.why: A suitable demonstration or example supports the claim that the atmosphere exerts pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a relevant example, such as atmospheric pressure crushing a can as it cools.

modelAnswer: The atmosphere exerts pressure because air has weight.
For example, when a heated tin can containing a little water is cooled, atmospheric pressure can crush it.

items.followUp: How does torque change if the applied force is doubled while the moment arm stays constant?

rubric.why: Torque depends on the applied force and its perpendicular moment arm.
rubric.description: Relates torque to force and moment arm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the relation torque = force × moment arm.

rubric.why: At constant force, doubling the moment arm doubles the torque.
rubric.description: States the effect of doubling the moment arm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the torque doubles.

modelAnswer: If the force remains constant and the moment arm is doubled, the torque doubles.
